title: You Think Cash Rewards Boost Drive, Yet Paying for Play Makes Your Brain Quit for Good
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Edward Deci (1971): Soma Puzzle Cubes, Overjustification & How Cash Rewards Undermine Intrinsic Motivation, grounded in Edward L. Deci (1971) (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that in 1971 at the University of Rochester, Edward Deci invited 24 college students across three one-hour sessions to assemble three-dimensional 'Soma' block puzzles (invented by Piet Hein) into sketched shapes.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how basal ganglia, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that in Session 1, nobody was paid; halfway through each session, Deci excused himself for 8 minutes leaving current magazines (New Yorker, Playboy, Time) right beside the Soma blocks while secretly timing through a one-way mirror how many seconds students played with the puzzles FOR FUN.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Edward L. Deci (1971). Effects of externally mediated rewards on intrinsic motivation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0030644
- Kerri P. Peters, Emma Grauerholz-Fisher, Timothy R. Vollmer, Angie Van Arsdale (2022). An evaluation of the overjustification hypothesis: A replication of Deci (1971). Behavior Analysis: Research and Practice. https://doi.org/10.1037/bar0000245
- Mark R. Lepper, David Greene, Richard E. Nisbett (1973). Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward: A test of the "overjustification" hypothesis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0035519

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
